did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title identifies it as “A Psalm of David” and dedicates it to the chief musician. It serves as an introduction to the psalm and is not part of the prayer itself.
Did you know? The prayer addresses the king in the singular and asks that the Lord answer him in the day of trouble and protect him by the name of the God of Jacob.
Did you know? Help is described as coming both from the sanctuary and from Zion, linking divine assistance with the holy place.
Did you know? The worshipers ask the Lord to remember the king’s offerings and burnt offering—that is, his gifts and sacrifice.
Did you know? The request for the king includes both his heart’s desires and his plans, asking that the Lord grant them all.
Did you know? After the requests for help comes a response of joy and confidence: the people will shout for joy over the Lord’s salvation and rally under the banner of their God’s name.
Did you know? This verse marks a transition from prayer to confidence: the speaker declares that he knows the Lord has saved His anointed one—the king who was anointed to rule.
Did you know? The psalm contrasts relying on chariots and horses with relying on the name of the Lord, the God of Israel; military power is set against faith.
Did you know? The result of this contrast is described as a reversal: the enemies bow down and fall, while the worshipers rise and stand firm.
Did you know? The psalm ends by returning to a direct appeal to the Lord: “Lord, save!” It asks that the King answer us on the day we call to Him.
